notes.front: What is Looker?
notes.back: A Google Cloud product for exploring, sharing and visualising your company's data, so that you can make better business decisions.
notes.explanation: The documentation frames its purpose around company data and better business decisions.
notes.example: Like a shared set of charts on the office wall, but people can click into any chart to ask their own follow-up question.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Looker”, introduction
notes.evidence: Looker is a product that helps you explore, share, and visualize your company's data so that you can make better business decisions.

notes.front: What is streaming analytics?
notes.back: Processing and analysing data records continuously, as they are generated, instead of waiting for delayed batches.
notes.explanation: The study guide ties it to reacting to time-sensitive events with the most up-to-date data.
notes.example: Like a live football score that updates with every goal, rather than a results table printed the next morning.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Pub/Sub?
notes.back: An asynchronous, scalable messaging service that separates the services that produce messages from the services that process them.
notes.explanation: Services talk to each other asynchronously through it, with latencies typically around 100 milliseconds.
notes.example: Like a noticeboard: the person pinning a note doesn't wait for readers, and any number of readers can pick it up.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Pub/Sub?”, introduction
notes.evidence: Pub/Sub is an asynchronous and scalable messaging service that decouples services producing messages from services processing those messages. Pub/Sub allows services to communicate asynchronously, with latencies typically on the order of 100 milliseconds.

notes.front: What is Dataflow?
notes.back: A Google Cloud service for unified stream and batch data processing at scale, through pipelines that read, transform and write data.
notes.explanation: ‘Unified’ means the same service handles data that arrives continuously and data processed in batches.
notes.example: Like a factory conveyor: raw goods come in one end, get cleaned and sorted on the way, and are packed at the other end.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Dataflow overview”, introduction
notes.evidence: Dataflow is a Google Cloud service that provides unified stream and batch data processing at scale. Use Dataflow to create data pipelines that read from one or more sources, transform the data, and write the data to a destination.

notes.front: What is Apache Beam, in relation to Dataflow?
notes.back: The open source project Dataflow is built on; you write pipelines with Beam's language-specific kits and Dataflow runs them.
notes.explanation: Beam supports Java, Python and Go, and Dataflow executes the pipelines written with it.
notes.example: Like a recipe written in a standard format: any well-equipped kitchen can cook it, and Dataflow is one such kitchen.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Dataflow overview”, “Portable with Apache Beam”
notes.evidence: Dataflow is built on the open source Apache Beam project. Apache Beam lets you write pipelines using a language-specific SDK. Apache Beam supports Java, Python, and Go SDKs, as well as multi-language pipelines. Dataflow executes Apache Beam pipelines.

notes.front: What is Managed Service for Apache Spark?
notes.back: Google Cloud's managed service for running Apache Spark and Hadoop clusters.
notes.explanation: Being managed means you can use these clusters without an administrator or special software.
notes.example: Like hiring a fully staffed workshop by the minute, instead of buying and maintaining your own machine tools.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Managed Service for Apache Spark on clusters overview”, “Advantages”
notes.evidence: Managed — Use Spark and Hadoop clusters without the assistance of an administrator or special software.

notes.front: Which older product names does “Managed Service for Apache Spark” replace?
notes.back: “Dataproc on Compute Engine” (cluster deployment) and “Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark” (serverless deployment).
notes.explanation: The one new name covers both the cluster and the serverless ways of running Spark.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Managed Service for Apache Spark on clusters overview”, name notice
notes.evidence: "Managed Service for Apache Spark" is the new name for the product formerly known as "Dataproc on Compute Engine" (cluster deployment) and "Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark" (serverless deployment).

notes.front: In the study guide's terms, how does Looker democratise data?
notes.back: It lets anyone explore data and answer their own questions, without needing technical expertise.
notes.explanation: The study guide links this to organisations being able to find and act on insights straight away.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does pairing Looker with a database such as BigQuery let an organisation do, according to the study guide?
notes.back: Build real-time reports and dashboards, and feed data into everyday workflows.
notes.explanation: The study guide gives BigQuery as its example of a Structured Query Language database for Looker to work with.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does real-time streaming matter to a business, according to the study guide?
notes.back: It lets the organisation react at once to time-sensitive events, with decisions based on the freshest data available.
notes.explanation: The study guide sets this against waiting for traditional, delayed batches of data.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does batch processing differ from streaming analytics?
notes.back: Batch processing handles large volumes at once, often with long delays; streaming processes records continuously as they arrive.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud notes that streaming suits sources that send small pieces of data, often kilobytes, in a continuous flow.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is streaming analytics?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In ecommerce, what does the study guide say streamed clickstream data can be used for?
notes.back: Optimising the shopping experience with real-time pricing, promotions and stock management.
notes.explanation: It is one of three industry examples in the study guide, alongside financial services and news media.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In financial services, what does the study guide say streamed account activity can be used for?
notes.back: Spotting abnormal behaviour in the data stream and raising a security alert.
notes.explanation: The alert comes from analysing account activity as it streams in, not from a later report.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In news media, how does the study guide say streamed click records are used?
notes.back: They are enriched with demographic information so that more relevant articles can be served to the target audience.
notes.explanation: Enrichment here means adding other data, in this case demographic details, to the streamed clicks before acting on them.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Pub/Sub, what are publishers and subscribers?
notes.back: Publishers are event producers; subscribers are event consumers. Publishers broadcast events asynchronously instead of calling subscribers directly.
notes.explanation: In direct remote calls the sender waits for the receiver; broadcasting removes that wait and makes the system more flexible and robust.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Pub/Sub?”, introduction
notes.evidence: In systems communicating through RPCs, publishers must wait for subscribers to receive the data. However, the asynchronous integration in Pub/Sub increases the flexibility and robustness of the overall system.

notes.front: Pub/Sub is used for {{c1::streaming analytics}} and data integration pipelines to load and distribute data.
notes.explanation: It can also act as messaging middleware between services or as a queue that spreads tasks out in parallel.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Pub/Sub?”, introduction
notes.evidence: Pub/Sub is used for streaming analytics and data integration pipelines to load and distribute data. It's equally effective as a messaging-oriented middleware for service integration or as a queue to parallelize tasks.

notes.front: What does it mean that Dataflow is fully managed?
notes.back: Google allocates the worker machines for each job and deletes them when it ends; you don't provision or manage them.
notes.explanation: You are billed for the compute resources the job uses, not for machines you keep running yourself.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Dataflow overview”, “Managed data processing”
notes.evidence: When you run a Dataflow job, the Dataflow service allocates a pool of worker VMs to execute the pipeline. You don't need to provision or manage these VMs. When the job completes or is cancelled, Dataflow automatically deletes the VMs. You're billed for the compute resources that your job uses.

notes.front: How does Dataflow cope when a pipeline's workload grows or shrinks?
notes.back: It autoscales: it adds worker machines, or shuts some down if fewer are needed.
notes.explanation: Data is processed in parallel, with the work spread across many worker machines.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Dataflow overview”, “Scalable data pipelines”
notes.evidence: Data is processed in parallel, so the work is distributed across multiple VMs. Dataflow can autoscale by provisioning extra worker VMs, or by shutting down some worker VMs if fewer are needed.

notes.front: A retailer's regional managers keep waiting days for the data team to answer simple sales questions. They want to explore the numbers themselves, without learning to code. Which Google Cloud product fits best?
notes.back: A) Looker
notes.choices:
A) Looker
B) Pub/Sub
C) Dataflow
D) Managed Service for Apache Spark
notes.choicesExplained: B) Pub/Sub moves messages between services; it gives managers nothing to explore. C) Dataflow builds processing pipelines, a job for engineers. D) Managed Service for Apache Spark runs Spark and Hadoop clusters, again an engineering tool.
notes.explanation: The study guide presents Looker as the tool that lets non-specialists explore data and answer their own questions.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A delivery firm keeps its order data in BigQuery and wants operations staff to watch up-to-the-minute dashboards and act on them in their daily work. What does the study guide suggest?
notes.back: B) Pair Looker with BigQuery for real-time reports, dashboards and workflows
notes.choices:
A) Export the data weekly to spreadsheets
B) Pair Looker with BigQuery for real-time reports, dashboards and workflows
C) Run a nightly Managed Service for Apache Spark job
D) Send each order through Pub/Sub to staff mailboxes
notes.choicesExplained: A) Weekly exports are the opposite of up to the minute. D) Pub/Sub delivers events between services, not dashboards to people. C) A nightly job is batch work, so the dashboards would lag by a day.
notes.explanation: The study guide names this pairing as the way to get real-time reports and dashboards and to bring data into workflows.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of these tasks most needs streaming analytics rather than batch processing?
notes.back: B) Flagging a suspicious card payment while the customer is still at the till
notes.choices:
A) Producing last year's annual sales report
B) Flagging a suspicious card payment while the customer is still at the till
C) Archiving a month of old log files
D) Recalculating quarterly staff bonuses
notes.choicesExplained: A) An annual report looks back over a closed period, so a batch is fine. C) Archiving old logs has no time pressure. D) Quarterly bonuses are worked out once per quarter, which suits batch processing.
notes.explanation: Only the payment check loses its value if the answer arrives late; the others can wait for a batch.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A game studio has thousands of servers emitting player events. It wants a service that collects these events from many sources at once and hands them to several downstream systems, without the senders waiting on the receivers. Which product fits?
notes.back: D) Pub/Sub
notes.choices:
A) Looker
B) BigQuery
C) Dataflow
D) Pub/Sub
notes.choicesExplained: A) Looker presents data to people; it does not collect events. B) BigQuery stores and queries data at the end of a pipeline. C) Dataflow transforms data in a pipeline, often reading from Pub/Sub, but is not the messaging layer.
notes.explanation: Publishers hand events to Pub/Sub without waiting, and Pub/Sub delivers them to all the services that react to them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “What is Pub/Sub?”, introduction
notes.evidence: Publishers send events to the Pub/Sub service, without regard to how or when these events are to be processed. Pub/Sub then delivers events to all the services that react to them.

notes.front: An insurer wants one managed pipeline service that cleans and aggregates both last year's stored claims and today's live claims before loading them into BigQuery. Which product fits best?
notes.back: D) Dataflow
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Storage
B) Pub/Sub
C) Looker
D) Dataflow
notes.choicesExplained: B) Pub/Sub carries messages but does not clean or aggregate them. C) Looker shows data once it is loaded. A) Cloud Storage stores files; it does not process them.
notes.explanation: Dataflow processes stream and batch data with one programming model and writes the results to a destination such as BigQuery.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Dataflow overview”, introduction
notes.evidence: Dataflow is a Google Cloud service that provides unified stream and batch data processing at scale.

notes.front: A bank runs dozens of existing Apache Spark and Hadoop jobs in its own data centre and wants to move them to Google Cloud without rewriting them or running clusters by hand. Which product fits best?
notes.back: C) Managed Service for Apache Spark
notes.choices:
A) Pub/Sub
B) Looker
C) Managed Service for Apache Spark
D) Dataflow, after rewriting every job in Apache Beam
notes.choicesExplained: A) Pub/Sub is messaging, not a place to run Spark jobs. B) Looker explores data; it does not run processing jobs. D) Rewriting every job is exactly what the bank wants to avoid.
notes.explanation: Existing projects can move to it without redevelopment, so the jobs need not be rewritten.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Managed Service for Apache Spark on clusters overview”, “Advantages”
notes.evidence: which lets you move existing projects into Managed Service for Apache Spark on clusters without redevelopment.

notes.front: In Google's typical Dataflow pipeline, how do the jobs of Pub/Sub, Dataflow and Looker differ?
notes.back: Pub/Sub takes in the data; Dataflow reads it, may transform it, and writes it to BigQuery; Looker gives insights from BigQuery.
notes.explanation: BigQuery sits between Dataflow and Looker as the data warehouse that analysts can query.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Dataflow overview”, “How data pipelines work”
notes.evidence: Pub/Sub ingests data from an external system. - Dataflow reads the data from Pub/Sub and writes it to BigQuery. During this stage, Dataflow might transform or aggregate the data. - BigQuery acts as a data warehouse, allowing data analysts to run ad hoc queries on the data. - Looker provides real-time BI insights from the data stored in BigQuery.
